sense.text:
“as his custom was, he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day, and stood up for to read.” Christ is at Nazareth, where he was brought up, beginning the public reading described here at thirty years old. The Sabbath setting matters: he opens the prophets to announce his mission, rather than introducing a different message detached from them.

“And there was delivered unto him the book of the prophet Esaias. And when he had opened the book, he found the place where it was written,” Esaias is Isaiah. The place he finds is Isaiah 61, which is opened next to examine the words individually. Gospel means good news, good tidings, or glad tidings; the introductory explanation of the old word Godspell connects it with a good story or message.

“The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised,” These are the conditions in which our people must recognize themselves: poor, brokenhearted, captive, blind, and bruised. Liberation is good news to people who need release, not a description of people already ruling and enjoying freedom.

Black liberation here includes the scattered tribes identified among Latinos, Native American Indians, and the people of the Pacific, not only Black Americans. Church teaching can leave a person unable to see his own people in these words. The question is whether we recognize our condition when we hear the promise.

“To preach the acceptable year of the Lord.” Isaiah 61 will explain that acceptable year together with meekness, healing, captivity, prison, and mourning. The words in Luke and Isaiah concern the same mission and must be understood together.

“And he began to say unto them, This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears.” After reading, Christ closes the book, gives it back to the minister, and sits down. Everyone in the synagogue has his eyes fixed on him. He then identifies himself with the work just announced: the Spirit, the gospel, the healing, and the deliverance are not disconnected promises about somebody else.

That declaration is the reason for returning to Isaiah 61. Luke 4:18-19 gives the mission, and Isaiah supplies the words that will be examined carefully so our people can see who needs that good news and what liberation involves.

“The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me; because the Lord hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek;” Good tidings means gospel, good news. Meek means "those that submit themselves to God's will." The definition includes humility, gentleness, and submission, not being soft or listening to every idiot on the street. "Meekness is strength under control"—God's control. Patience does not mean having no self-assertiveness. Moses submitted to God's will completely; strength, putting others before oneself, and reliance on God's justice belong together.

“he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted,” Brokenhearted means "deep grief, spiritual bankruptcy, and crushed spirit." The definition describes emotional and spiritual ruin: pain, despair, loss, helplessness, a shattered inner self needing God. Recognition of that need leads to humility and repentance, and God promises healing and restoration. Our people have been broken by slavery, including the loss of language, heritage, and identity. Demanding that they pull themselves up by their bootstraps ignores what was taken from them: "You stole our boots." Their cry for reparations expresses that wounded condition. Revelation's wiping away of tears promises the end of its causes, not simply a nicer feeling about them.

“to proclaim liberty to the captives,” A captive is "one taken in war." The definition includes cruel treatment, people sold as slaves, and removal into foreign countries. That is why literal enslavement cannot be replaced with an explanation that everybody is captive in exactly the same way. The comparison with paid indentured labour is used to distinguish it from being brought in chains against one's will. Luke describes Israel carried into all nations; Solomon explains that sin brought the captivity and that remembering our identity, confessing wickedness, and repenting belong to deliverance.

“and the opening of the prison to them that are bound;” Prison has physical and spiritual dimensions. The definition includes confinement, punishment, pits, and spiritual bondage. The ghettos and the violence within them can become so familiar that oppression looks normal and the prison is simply called home. America and the other lands of captivity remain foreign lands governed by others' laws; taking off chains did not itself restore our own land or government. Opening blind eyes includes recognizing that condition.

Bound also means enslavement to sin. A good job and decent money can make someone insist that he is not captive, just as comfortable men under Rome denied bondage. Hosea's bound-up iniquity leads into John 8: the sin that brought captivity and the captivity itself both need to be removed. Christ's liberty addresses both.

precepts.why:
“(Now the man Moses was very meek, above all the men which were upon the face of the earth.)” Moses is the example used while defining the meek who receive Isaiah's good tidings. He submitted to God's will "100%." His meekness did not mean that he was soft, unable to lead, or obliged to listen to every foolish person on the street.

The definition is humility, gentleness, and submission to God's will. "Meekness is strength under control"—and the control is God's. Moses led the Israelites with patience and reliance on God. Putting others before oneself and trusting God's sovereignty and justice require controlled strength, not weakness. That is the meekness required of all of us, rather than the mistaken idea that submission to God means having no firmness.

“But the meek shall inherit the earth; and shall delight themselves in the abundance of peace.” This is the inheritance attached to the definition of meekness. The promise joins inheriting the land with delight in abundant peace. Those who submit themselves to God's will are not being told that captivity and dispossession are the reward for obeying him.

The surrounding definition distinguishes humility from weakness and describes strength under God's control. Moses supplies the example of that character; this promise supplies its reward. Isaiah's good tidings are therefore addressed to people whose submission leads to God's blessing and inheritance. The corresponding blessing in Matthew carries the same point into Christ's words.

“Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth.” The explanation is explicit: the meek are "those that submit themselves to God's will." This blessing follows the definition of humility, gentleness, and controlled strength, not a definition of helplessness or cowardice.

As part of the Beatitudes, the promise gives an inheritance to the people who embody that submission. It agrees with the meek inheriting the land in Psalms and with the good tidings preached to the meek in Isaiah. Meekness is not an instruction to make oppression our permanent home. It is the character of those who receive God's promised blessing and inheritance.

“For the Lamb which is in the midst of the throne shall feed them, and shall lead them unto living fountains of waters: and God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes.” The Lamb is Christ. He feeds us and leads us to living fountains of waters; God is the one who finally wipes away all the tears. That last promise answers the brokenheartedness in Isaiah, whose definition includes deep grief, spiritual bankruptcy, and a crushed spirit.

The continuing need to have tears wiped away shows the condition of the Israelites awaiting that deliverance. Our people's grief is not imaginary or already over. Slavery and oppression have left a brokenhearted people, and the gospel announces God's care for them. The move into Revelation 21 makes the result more explicit: the conditions producing those tears will pass away.

“And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away.” Each part of the promise is emphasized: no more death, no more sorrow, no more crying, and no more pain. These are the things afflicting the brokenhearted people addressed in Isaiah 61.

The "former things" are explained as oppression, captivity, and poverty. God wiping away tears means those causes of grief are done away with, not that our people are expected to keep living in them forever while merely being told to feel better. Read after the Lamb feeding and leading his people in Revelation 7, this gives the full direction of the comfort: provision, release, and an end to the suffering that has crushed their spirit.

“And they shall fall by the edge of the sword, and shall be led away captive into all nations: and Jerusalem shall be trodden down of the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles be fulfilled.” The sword is identified as Rome's sword against the Israelites. The words about being led away captive into all nations explain whose captivity Isaiah promises to end. The people were conquered and removed, not simply experiencing a private feeling of spiritual restriction.

The captivity did not stop at AD 70. Its continuation is traced through Spain, France, Britain, and America: the same curse extends through the lands of the dispersion. Jerusalem being trodden down until the Gentiles' times are fulfilled also describes continuing foreign dominion. That is why "liberty to the captives" must include the release of our scattered people from the condition Christ describes here.

“If they sin against thee, (for there is no man that sinneth not,) and thou be angry with them, and deliver them to the enemy, so that they carry them away captives unto the land of the enemy, far or near;” Solomon describes God becoming angry because the people sin and delivering them to an enemy, who takes them captive into the enemy's land, far or near. America is the present example of that foreign land; the people were not brought there as its rulers.

“Yet if they shall bethink themselves in the land whither they were carried captives, and repent, and make supplication unto thee in the land of them that carried them captives, saying, We have sinned, and have done perversely, we have committed wickedness;” To bethink ourselves is to remember who we are: the twelve tribes of Israel. Repentance and supplication must accompany that remembrance, including confession that we have sinned, done perversely, and committed wickedness.

That is the process our people must undertake now. The promise of liberty does not disconnect our literal captivity from the commandments we broke. Solomon supplies both the reason for the captivity and the response required of the people seeking deliverance.

“I have raised him up in righteousness, and I will direct all his ways: he shall build my city, and he shall let go my captives, not for price nor reward, saith the Lord of hosts.” The words singled out are the building of God's city and the release of "my captives," not for price or reward. God directs the work in righteousness and declares what will happen to the people he calls his own.

This continues the explanation of Isaiah's liberty to the captives. After Solomon's description of Israel carried into an enemy's land and called to repent, the emphasis here is the promised release. The captives are people who have actually been held; their freedom is not merely a different attitude toward confinement. The following reading in Isaiah 49 develops the same assurance: even the power of a mighty captor cannot prevent the Lord from delivering them.

“But thus saith the Lord, Even the captives of the mighty shall be taken away, and the prey of the terrible shall be delivered: for I will contend with him that contendeth with thee, and I will save thy children.” Israel is the prey, not the power holding the prey. Assyria and Babylon are named as terrible powers in the earlier setting; America, Spain, Portugal, and Europe are named in the application to the present captivity. The "mighty" captor is identified with the white ruling power that has contended against our people.

God promises to contend with that opponent and to save Israel's children. The force of the promise is that even those held by a mighty power can be delivered; the captor is not stronger than the God making that declaration.

“And I will feed them that oppress thee with their own flesh; and they shall be drunken with their own blood, as with sweet wine: and all flesh shall know that I the Lord am thy Saviour and thy Redeemer, the mighty One of Jacob.” The flesh and blood describe severe judgment on the oppressors. The closing identification is essential: the Saviour and Redeemer is the mighty One of Jacob. Jacob means the Israelites. Oppressor and oppressed cannot both be treated as the same party in this promise; Isaiah's liberty concerns Jacob's people being rescued from those oppressing them.

“And ye shall seek me, and find me, when ye shall search for me with all your heart.” Our people seeking the Lord now are the application of this promise. Seeking must be with the whole heart, not a casual demand for relief without turning back to him.

“And I will be found of you, saith the Lord: and I will turn away your captivity, and I will gather you from all the nations, and from all the places whither I have driven you, saith the Lord; and I will bring you again into the place whence I caused you to be carried away captive.” God promises to be found, turn the captivity, and gather the people from all the nations and all the places where he drove them. He also promises to bring them again to the place from which they were carried captive.

That gathering and return explain liberty in Isaiah 61. The people are scattered in actual countries, and the promised reversal is an actual return. It belongs with Solomon's instruction to remember who we are, repent, confess our sin, and make supplication while still in the land of captivity.

“Happy is he that hath the God of Jacob for his help, whose hope is in the Lord his God:” The identification is the God of Jacob. That keeps the following promises connected to Jacob's children rather than leaving the oppressed, hungry, and prisoners undefined.

“Which made heaven, and earth, the sea, and all that therein is: which keepeth truth for ever:” The one who helps Jacob is also the maker of heaven, earth, and sea, keeping truth for ever. His power and faithfulness stand behind what follows.

“Which executeth judgment for the oppressed: which giveth food to the hungry. The Lord looseth the prisoners:” Jacob's children would be oppressed, would need food, and would be prisoners. Their hunger includes physical food and spiritual nourishment; both are needed. The Lord loosing those prisoners is part of the gospel being explained in Isaiah 61. Justice for the oppressed, provision for the hungry, and release from prison are joined in the same work of restoration.

“They that see thee shall narrowly look upon thee, and consider thee, saying, Is this the man that made the earth to tremble, that did shake kingdoms;” Lucifer is identified here as the king of Babylon, a man rather than an invisible spiritual demon. The application is to the white imperial ruler making the earth tremble with bombs and shaking kingdoms through wars. Bombing Somalia and the remarks about Somali immigrants are contemporary examples used to illustrate that claim.

“That made the world as a wilderness, and destroyed the cities thereof; that opened not the house of his prisoners?” The prison house is identified as America. Destroyed cities and a world made like a wilderness are connected with the refusal to release the prisoners. This answers Isaiah 61's promise that the prison will be opened.

The discussion of Somalis, Haitians, Jamaicans, Puerto Ricans, and Dominicans focuses on divisions between our people: newcomers may look down on Black Americans, then learn through their own affliction that they need one another. The historical illustration concerns Black Americans seeking to join Ethiopians against Italy and restrictions placed on that travel. The visit to Israel supplies another illustration: American, Ethiopian, and other African Black communities kept apart. The conclusion is "divide and conquer"—keep the groups separate so they do not unite. Opening the prison includes recognizing both the confinement and those divisions.

“To open the blind eyes, to bring out the prisoners from the prison, and them that sit in darkness out of the prison house.” The blind eyes are spiritually blind: our people may be unable to see that the place they call home is a prison. They were brought to America against their will, and the chains are evidence of that arrival as prisoners.

Taking off the chains did not make the people rulers in their own land. Living in someone else's land, under someone else's rules and laws, is the distinction drawn against the declaration "Free at last." A condition can become so normal that the captive no longer recognizes it.

The prison is not limited to America. It includes all the lands where Israel was made captive. Those sitting in darkness need their eyes opened and need to be brought out of the prison house. Isaiah 61's release therefore has a spiritual dimension without erasing the physical captivity.

“As for thee also, by the blood of thy covenant I have sent forth thy prisoners out of the pit wherein is no water.” The blood of the covenant is Christ dying on the cross. The prisoners are our people, and the pit is America and the other countries where we are scattered. No water means no truth in that pit.

“Turn you to the strong hold, ye prisoners of hope: even to day do I declare that I will render double unto thee;” The stronghold is the Bible. We are "prisoners of hope," always hoping for something better, and are told where to turn. The promise of a double return means the present pit is not the final condition.

“When I have bent Judah for me, filled the bow with Ephraim, and raised up thy sons, O Zion, against thy sons, O Greece, and made thee as the sword of a mighty man.” Judah is the bow bent for God, Ephraim fills the bow, and the remaining tribes are the sons of Zion. Their being raised against Greece and made like the sword of a mighty man is treated as still future, not already fulfilled. Release from captivity leads into the restored role appointed to Israel. That imagery is returned to when Ezekiel describes God's vengeance by the hand of his people.

“The iniquity of Ephraim is bound up; his sin is hid.” Bound is not only a word for chains around the body. Ephraim's iniquity is bound up, and his sin is hid; the spiritual bondage under discussion includes enslavement to sin.

The distinction matters for a person who has a good job and makes decent money, then says he cannot be captive. Personal comfort does not answer the nation's condition or remove the sin involved. The definition of being bound covers literal restraint as well as spiritual bondage.

This reading leads directly into John 8. The truth making us free has both a literal and a spiritual meaning: sin brought the captivity, so freedom from sin and freedom from bondage cannot be separated in explaining Isaiah's promise.

sense.text:
“And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.” The truth makes us free in two connected senses, literal and spiritual. This reading follows the definitions of prison and being bound in Isaiah 61, including Hosea's iniquity bound up. It does not replace the physical captivity with an entirely spiritual explanation.

The verses that follow show why both must remain in view. Men who are comfortable under a foreign ruler deny bondage; Christ answers by exposing the sin that makes a servant. Deuteronomy then supplies the consequence of that sin: the people and their children going into captivity.

“They answered him, We be Abraham’s seed, and were never in bondage to any man: how sayest thou, Ye shall be made free?” These men answer as Abraham's seed and insist they have never been in bondage. Their wealth and comfortable lives prevent them from recognizing what Rome's dominion and yearly taxes mean. Rome is over them even when their personal circumstances feel prosperous.

That is the same mistake as saying a good job proves we are not captive now. Their answer is called "arrogant talk": they hear Christ's promise of freedom but will not acknowledge the condition from which they need to be delivered. National bondage is not cancelled by an individual's money.

“Jesus answered them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin.” Christ brings the answer into its spiritual context: whoever commits sin serves sin. But the result of Israel sinning is also captivity and bondage. The spiritual explanation therefore does not deny the literal one.

Deuteronomy 28 is read to establish that connection. Refusing God's voice and commandments brings the curses; among them are children handed to another people and children going into captivity. Breaking God's commandments is sin, and that disobedience produces the national bondage. Freedom must deal with the cause as well as its consequence.

“And the servant abideth not in the house for ever: but the Son abideth ever.” The reading continues from the servant's position to the Son's lasting place in the house, then gives the promise: “If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.”

"Free from sin, free from bondage" is the conclusion. These are not competing explanations. The captivity described in Deuteronomy came through disobedience, so the Son's freedom must answer both. The men disputing with Christ could not see that connection because they first refused to recognize their bondage under Rome.

precepts.why:
“But it shall come to pass, if thou wilt not hearken unto the voice of the Lord thy God, to observe to do all his commandments and his statutes which I command thee this day; that all these curses shall come upon thee, and overtake thee:” The starting point is refusal to hear God and do his commandments and statutes. Sin is breaking those commandments, and the curses overtake the people as the result.

“Thy sons and thy daughters shall be given unto another people, and thine eyes shall look, and fail with longing for them all the day long: and there shall be no might in thine hand.” Sons and daughters are given to another people; the parents long for them but have no power to recover them. This is the slavery being connected to sin, not merely a feeling of being spiritually troubled.

“Thou shalt beget sons and daughters, but thou shalt not enjoy them; for they shall go into captivity.” Captivity means parents cannot enjoy the children they have brought forth. The two readings make the cause and consequence plain: serving sin brings literal bondage. Returning to John 8, Christ's promise to make us free addresses both the sin and the captivity that followed it.

sense.text:
“To proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of vengeance of our God; to comfort all that mourn;” There is a particular year and a particular day appointed. The vengeance answers what verse 1 described: brokenheartedness, captivity, prison, and bondage. The good news includes God's judgment ending those conditions, rather than promising that oppression will continue indefinitely.

The definition of vengeance is "retribution or punishment inflicted in response to wrongdoing." It joins divine justice with the response to injustice and is tied to God's holiness and the moral order he established. The cries for justice from the mothers of Rasheem Carter, Kendrick Johnson, and Sonya Massey illustrate the grief being discussed. The demand for justice cannot be separated from the wrong that produced it.

Vengeance begins with the Lord. Christ first overcomes the opposing armies; Ezekiel then gives Israel the role God appoints. A commentary that says vengeance belongs to God must not be used to erase the words about its being executed by the hand of Israel.

Mourning is "deep sorrow or grief," associated with death, loss, or repentance, and includes personal and communal lamentation. Jeremiah's continual tears show that grief over the destruction of our people. The instruction is to wait for the Lord, not jump up and act against others. The readings that follow promise an answer to the cry, teachers showing the way, a return to Zion, and sorrow giving way to everlasting joy.

precepts.why:
“And I will lay my vengeance upon Edom by the hand of my people Israel: and they shall do in Edom according to mine anger and according to my fury; and they shall know my vengeance, saith the Lord God.” The crucial words are "by the hand of my people Israel." Vengeance belongs to God, but that does not mean he assigns Israel no part in its execution. The anger, fury, and vengeance remain his throughout the verse.

The order is explained before the reading: Christ first breaks through the armies of the world. "The Lord's going to get his lick first" expresses that initial overthrow. The role subsequently given to Israel agrees with Zechariah 9, where Judah, Ephraim, and Zion are made into a weapon.

This is the appointed future vengeance answering Isaiah's captives and mourners, not an instruction for listeners to begin violence now. The later explanation of Lamentations is explicit that we must wait for the Lord's return.

“For I lift up my hand to heaven, and say, I live for ever.” God lifts his hand to heaven and declares that he lives for ever. The next words announce his judgment: “If I whet my glittering sword, and mine hand take hold on judgment; I will render vengeance to mine enemies, and will reward them that hate me.”

Whet means sharpen. The sharpened, glittering sword and the hand taking hold on judgment introduce repayment to God's enemies and those who hate him. “I will make mine arrows drunk with blood, and my sword shall devour flesh; and that with the blood of the slain and of the captives, from the beginning of revenges upon the enemy.” The blood and devouring sword express the severity of that repayment.

“Rejoice, O ye nations, with his people: for he will avenge the blood of his servants, and will render vengeance to his adversaries, and will be merciful unto his land, and to his people.” The closing point is the blood of his servants being avenged, vengeance rendered to his adversaries, and mercy shown to his land and people. This is why judgment and comfort belong together in Isaiah 61. The same act that repays the enemies ends the suffering of those they afflicted.

“For it is the day of the Lord’s vengeance, and the year of recompences for the controversy of Zion.” Recompences means "paybacks"—"the big payback." The day and the year repeat the language of Isaiah 61:2. This is an appointed judgment, not an expectation that the present order will simply turn into peace and goodwill without an accounting for what was done to the twelve tribes.

The controversy of Zion is explained by two questions: who are the Israelites, and to whom does the land belong? Those disputes are connected with the treatment of our people. God's day of vengeance and year of payback answer that controversy. The coming recompense is therefore part of the good news to those who have been captive and have mourned.

“Strengthen ye the weak hands, and confirm the feeble knees.” Weak hands and feeble knees are applied to discouraged brothers and sisters who doubt they can endure. Strengthen the knees means stand up. The discussion applies that endurance to marriage, refusing adultery, modest dress, and the responsibilities of a wife and mother. Calling obedience a captivity or a cult does not remove those responsibilities; no one is locked inside the congregation.

“Say to them that are of a fearful heart, Be strong, fear not: behold, your God will come with vengeance, even God with a recompence; he will come and save you.” Fearful hearts are told to be strong, not because circumstances will soon become easy, but because God will come with vengeance and recompense. Recompense again means payback. The expectation is that conditions worsen before his saving intervention, so the promise must continually strengthen our people.

“And the ransomed of the Lord shall return, and come to Zion with songs and everlasting joy upon their heads: they shall obtain joy and gladness, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away.” Zion identifies the destination as the land of Israel and clarifies who is being ransomed. Songs and everlasting joy contrast with bullets and bombs in the land now, and with the sighing over bills and hardship in our present lives. The promised comfort is joy and gladness replacing sorrow, not merely continuing in fear.

“Who is this that cometh from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah? this that is glorious in his apparel, travelling in the greatness of his strength? I that speak in righteousness, mighty to save.” The one coming from Edom is identified as Christ, and Bozrah as Edom's capital. His glorious apparel is described as a beautiful, decked-out garment and armour, not an ordinary robe. He is mighty to save.

“Wherefore art thou red in thine apparel, and thy garments like him that treadeth in the winefat?” The red garment looks like the clothing of someone treading grapes. “I have trodden the winepress alone; and of the people there was none with me: for I will tread them in mine anger, and trample them in my fury; and their blood shall be sprinkled upon my garments, and I will stain all my raiment.” The winepress is explained as the judgment on Edom, with the blood of the slain staining his clothing. At this stage he acts alone: he does not need Israel's help in that initial overthrow.

“For the day of vengeance is in mine heart, and the year of my redeemed is come.” The day of vengeance and the year of the redeemed join judgment to our deliverance, just as Isaiah 61 does. The argument against treating Edom as a people already wholly gone is the expected return described here: whom would Christ be coming to judge? The waiting for that appointed day explains why vengeance and redemption are still anticipated.

“Seeing it is a righteous thing with God to recompense tribulation to them that trouble you;” Recompense means pay back. The New Testament calls that repayment righteous. Asking who troubles our people is not answered only by pointing at "Pooky and Ray Ray"; the discussion traces destructive behaviour to the system that shaped their environment, including ghettos and redlining.

They Cloned Tyrone supplies the illustration of people assigned destructive roles. The accompanying discussion of the "behavioral sync" experiment with mice claims that crowded conditions produced gangs, killing, and distorted behaviour before comparable conditions were imposed on our communities. That comparison is used to argue that the environment is part of the oppression being judged, not merely the individual offences visible inside it.

“And to you who are troubled rest with us, when the Lord Jesus shall be revealed from heaven with his mighty angels,” First recognize that we are a troubled people, then "rest with us in these scriptures." The invitation is to receive their comfort together. “In flaming fire taking vengeance on them that know not God, and that obey not the gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ:” The vengeance is connected back to Isaiah 61 and Isaiah 34; Edom and those following him are identified with the opposition described.

“Who shall be punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power;” “When he shall come to be glorified in his saints, and to be admired in all them that believe (because our testimony among you was believed) in that day.” Christ is glorified in his saints, identified as Israel, while those who reject the gospel face destruction. Rest and comfort do not erase judgment; these verses explain how both belong to the promised deliverance.

“All our enemies have opened their mouths against us.” “Fear and a snare is come upon us, desolation and destruction.” Enemies, fear, entrapment, desolation, and destruction give the setting for mourning. “Mine eye runneth down with rivers of water for the destruction of the daughter of my people.” The rivers of water are tears for the destruction of Jeremiah's people.

“Mine eye trickleth down, and ceaseth not, without any intermission,” He cannot stop crying; there is no intermission in his grief. That is a concrete picture of the "deep sorrow or grief" in the definition of mourning, not an abstract mood detached from the people's suffering.

“Till the Lord look down, and behold from heaven.” Jeremiah must wait for the Lord to look down from heaven. That is also the instruction when images of our people's destruction hurt inside and bring us to tears: "We can't jump up and do something." We must wait for the Lord to return. Isaiah's comfort promises God's answer to the sorrow; it does not authorize taking vengeance into our own hands now.

“For the people shall dwell in Zion at Jerusalem: thou shalt weep no more: he will be very gracious unto thee at the voice of thy cry; when he shall hear it, he will answer thee.” Zion at Jerusalem identifies the Israelites. The promise that they will weep no more also tells us their present condition: a weeping people repeatedly experiencing hardship. God hears the cry and answers graciously.

“And though the Lord give you the bread of adversity, and the water of affliction, yet shall not thy teachers be removed into a corner any more, but thine eyes shall see thy teachers:” The bread of adversity means hardship and hard times; the water of affliction is explained as tears over what we see and endure. The teachers no longer being removed into a corner is applied to the work in the streets and the classes held seven days a week, three times a day. Our people can see the teachers and hear instruction.

“And thine ears shall hear a word behind thee, saying, This is the way, walk ye in it, when ye turn to the right hand, and when ye turn to the left.” The voice showing the way addresses people walking in the wrong direction. Islam, Christianity, Buddhism, and other religions are named as the paths from which they need correction. Comfort includes being shown where to walk, not just having grief acknowledged. These promises explain the answer to mourning in Isaiah 61.

“Therefore the redeemed of the Lord shall return, and come with singing unto Zion; and everlasting joy shall be upon their head: they shall obtain gladness and joy; and sorrow and mourning shall flee away.” The redeemed return to the land, coming with singing unto Zion. Everlasting joy is upon their heads; gladness and joy replace the sorrow and mourning that now afflict the people.

This completes the sequence explaining Isaiah 61's comfort. Jeremiah showed the tears that continue while waiting for God; Isaiah 30 promised an answer to the cry and teachers directing the people; here the return itself is accompanied by singing. The promise is not simply relief for a moment while the captivity remains unchanged. It is a return and an enduring reversal of the condition that made our people mourn.

sense.text:
“To appoint unto them that mourn in Zion, to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness; that they might be called trees of righteousness, the planting of the Lord, that he might be glorified.” The identifying words are "them that mourn in Zion." Zion is another name for the twelve tribes of Israel. This sums up who has been addressed through the meek, brokenhearted, captives, prisoners, and mourners: the gospel concerns the restoration of that people.

Beauty for ashes, joy for mourning, and praise for heaviness describe the reversal of our people's condition. The images of Sonya Massey, Rasheem Carter, and the brother named Trey Reed are used to show why families mourn. The account questions official explanations of those deaths, including the account of Reed's death discussed alongside Colin Kaepernick's independent autopsy. The long list of other deaths, many not widely known, illustrates how loss can become normalized instead of recognized as suffering needing an answer.

The discussion also remembers Black political prisoners, not only recent deaths. The MOVE bombing in 1985 and Fred Hampton are examples connected with the treatment of liberation movements. The Black Panther Party and Black Liberation Army are named, together with Mumia Abu-Jamal, Assata Shakur, Sundiata Acoli, and Jalil Muntaqim. People who fought for rights can be forgotten while serving decades and dying in prison; the freedoms enjoyed by others must not make their confinement invisible.

Those are the conditions to which binding up the brokenhearted and opening the prison are applied. The people weighed down by them are promised righteousness as God's planting, for his glory. The contrast is a restoration of a people, not merely an improvement in an individual's mood.

“And as they heard these things, he added and spake a parable, because he was nigh to Jerusalem, and because they thought that the kingdom of God should immediately appear.” Being near Jerusalem, the people thought the kingdom would appear immediately. They expected the day of vengeance, the destruction of Rome, and Israel's liberation at that time. The parable is given because that expectation confuses the timing of Christ's mission.

The apostles' question about restoring the kingdom to Israel and John the Baptist's question from prison show the same expectation. John anticipated release, but Christ's works and his warning not to be offended gave encouragement while that deliverance had not come.

This was the time for Christ to be sacrificed, not yet the time for the national vengeance everyone wanted. The promise of liberation is not withdrawn; the first coming and the final overthrow must not be collapsed into the same moment.

precepts.why:
“When they therefore were come together, they asked of him, saying, Lord, wilt thou at this time restore again the kingdom to Israel?” The question is whether Christ will restore the kingdom to Israel "at this time." It confirms the expectation behind Luke 19:11: the people saw Christ and looked for the kingdom and the overthrow of their captors immediately.

The wording also identifies whose kingdom is to be restored. The apostles ask about Israel, not about an undefined kingdom belonging equally to every nation. Restoring it assumes a kingdom that Israel is to receive again.

The question therefore establishes both the people and the issue of timing. It is read before John's question from prison to show that he was not alone in expecting deliverance then. Understanding that expectation is necessary before following the nobleman's departure and later return in the parable.

“Now when John had heard in the prison the works of Christ, he sent two of his disciples,” “And said unto him, Art thou he that should come, or do we look for another?” John is in prison and expects deliverance. He had spoken boldly against Herod having his brother's wife and was arrested. His question is explained through the expectation that Christ would release him, not as proof that John was wicked.

“Jesus answered and said unto them, Go and shew John again those things which ye do hear and see:” “The blind receive their sight, and the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, and the poor have the gospel preached to them.” Christ sends encouragement through the works the disciples can hear and see: restored sight and hearing, walking, cleansing, raised dead, and the gospel preached to the poor.

“And blessed is he, whosoever shall not be offended in me.” The warning not to be offended answers John's disappointment in the timing. This is the time for Christ's sacrifice, not yet the time for vengeance and national deliverance. Israel wanted the deliverance part and did not want to hear about the sacrifice. That expectation explains both John's question and the belief in Luke 19 that the kingdom should appear immediately; it does not invalidate John's standing.

sense.text:
“Verily I say unto you, Among them that are born of women there hath not risen a greater than John the Baptist: notwithstanding he that is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.” Christ's testimony about John answers the accusation that he was wicked. No greater man born of women had risen; his question from prison must be read with that statement, not used to overturn it.

The least in the kingdom being greater is explained by the condition of the kingdom: righteousness without the fears and sin still present in John's life at that time. It does not mean John was an evil man. The following identification of him as Elijah and the appearance of Elijah with Moses reinforce the same point.

“And from the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven suffereth violence, and the violent take it by force.” The violence is against the kingdom on earth, the people of Israel, not a battle in the sky. Rome is the violent power taking it by force.

Pompey is named as the general who came with the Roman military and took Jerusalem around 63 BC. That conquest established Rome's hold on the land and explains why, when Christ was born, the people were paying taxes to Caesar. The earthly conquest is the point of the historical example: Israel is the kingdom suffering violence, which also explains why the people wanted Christ to destroy Rome and restore it.

“And if ye will receive it, this is Elias, which was for to come.” “He that hath ears to hear, let him hear.” Christ identifies John the Baptist as Elias, Elijah who was to come. The invitation to receive it and hear it means that John's identity must be taken from Christ's own explanation.

The reading backs up through John's greatness, the kingdom suffering violence, and the prophets and law prophesying until John before repeating this identification. It answers the effort to call John wicked because of his question in prison. Matthew 17 is then opened to show Elias appearing with Moses after John had already been killed.

precepts.why:
“And after six days Jesus taketh Peter, James, and John his brother, and bringeth them up into an high mountain apart,” Peter, James, and John accompany Christ up the mountain. John the Baptist has already been killed at this point, while Christ knows his own crucifixion is approaching.

“And was transfigured before them: and his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light.” “And, behold, there appeared unto them Moses and Elias talking with him.” His shining face, raiment white as light, and the appearance of Moses and Elias show the encounter witnessed by the disciples. Elias is connected directly to Christ's preceding identification of John the Baptist as Elijah.

The conclusion is that the disciples saw Christ speaking with Moses and John the Baptist in the spirit realm. That is used to reject the accusation that John was wicked. The John accompanying Peter and James is one of the witnesses; the identification of the already-dead Baptist concerns Elias appearing with Moses.

sense.text:
“because they thought that the kingdom of God should immediately appear.” The return to this verse adds Paul's warning against announcing Christ's day prematurely. The subject is Christ's coming and the gathering of the twelve tribes to him.

The falling away is explained as all twelve tribes falling and going into captivity. Judah, Benjamin, Levi, and remnants of the others were still in the land when Paul wrote; the Roman overthrow of AD 70 lay ahead. The man of sin also had to be revealed. Those intervening events explain why the anticipated deliverance was not immediate, even though everyone wanted it then.

“He said therefore, A certain nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom, and to return.” The nobleman is Christ. The far country is heaven, the true tabernacle, as shown by the reading of Acts in which a cloud receives him out of the disciples' sight.

The journey includes receiving a kingdom and returning. His going away explains the interval during which the servants are entrusted with work. It also corrects the expectation of an immediate kingdom: departure is part of the parable, and his return cannot be removed from its sequence.

“And he called his ten servants, and delivered them ten pounds, and said unto them, Occupy till I come.” The servants are Israel, identified by Isaiah's "Israel, art my servant" and Leviticus naming the children brought out of Egypt. The pounds are money in the story, but what they represent is more precious than currency: the word of God and the commandments.

The love of God's commandments above fine gold supplies that explanation. "Occupy till I come" means putting the understanding he has given to use while Christ is away. The question at his return will be what each servant did with it, not simply whether he kept possession of it.

“But his citizens hated him, and sent a message after him, saying, We will not have this man to reign over us.” The citizens refuse the nobleman's rule. Mark names the elders, chief priests, and scribes as the people who reject Christ; those leaders identify the hatred being explained.

That opposition must not be turned into the claim that every Israelite rejected him. The named opponents matter. Their refusal to have him reign also prepares for the later conclusion about enemies who persist in rejecting his authority.

“And it came to pass, that when he was returned, having received the kingdom, then he commanded these servants to be called unto him, to whom he had given the money, that he might know how much every man had gained by trading.” Receiving the kingdom contains more than the short wording of the parable first suggests. Isaiah's fire and chariots and Revelation's war show the judgment and overthrow preceding the announcement of the kingdom. It is not simply Christ returning to an uncontested throne.

After receiving it, he calls the servants to account. "What did you do with the understanding I imparted to you?" is the question represented by trading and gain. The judgment-seat reading makes that responsibility explicit for every man and every woman, whether the things done were good or bad.

“Then came the first, saying, Lord, thy pound hath gained ten pounds.” “And he said unto him, Well, thou good servant: because thou hast been faithful in a very little, have thou authority over ten cities.” A little entrusted to a faithful servant has produced an increase, and the reward is authority over ten cities. Faithfulness in little is the test for that larger responsibility.

The comparison is with a man trying to bring an out-of-order household into order: organizing a wife and children is already difficult, and governing ten cities is much more work. Those cities must learn the dietary, moral, civil, and ceremonial laws. The reward is therefore not an empty title or an easy task.

Revelation's rod of iron explains firm rule where people resist. Authority must establish God's laws, not leave the cities in their former disorder. Present faithfulness prepares the servant for that responsibility.

“And the second came, saying, Lord, thy pound hath gained five pounds.” The second servant has also made an increase, gaining five pounds. This introduces Matthew's rule that the one who has will receive more and have abundance.

Attention is then directed to the second half of that rule: even what an unproductive person has can be taken away. The five-pound gain is part of the contrast between servants who use the understanding entrusted to them and the servant who does nothing with it. Later, the gains are connected to differing responsibilities over cities.

“And another came, saying, Lord, behold, here is thy pound, which I have kept laid up in a napkin:” The napkin represents understanding or a gift left unused. Keeping it wrapped up is not the work Christ commanded and does not make the servant faithful.

Romans calls for fervency in God's business, John warns that the fruitless branch is taken away, and Ecclesiasticus exposes the sinner who refuses reproof and finds an excuse according to his will. Together they explain what is wrong with the napkin: inactivity is being defended instead of corrected. A fruitful person may be purged through trials to produce more; the unused gift is not an example of that productive endurance.

“For I feared thee, because thou art an austere man: thou takest up that thou layedst not down, and reapest that thou didst not sow.” Austere is defined as "stern and cold in appearance or manner," somber, grave, and especially "morally strict." "Christ was a cold brother" is the blunt description attached to that definition.

The servant uses that strictness as an excuse. Christ is not on the earth doing the work himself; the men entrusted with understanding must do it, and he returns to reap its benefit. Knowing what kind of lord he serves should move the servant to work, not supply a reason for wrapping the pound in a napkin.

“And he saith unto him, Out of thine own mouth will I judge thee, thou wicked servant. Thou knewest that I was an austere man, taking up that I laid not down, and reaping that I did not sow:” Christ calls him a wicked servant and judges him out of his own mouth. Knowing that his lord is morally strict does not excuse doing nothing. A man cannot assume that being an Israelite makes inactivity acceptable.

The reading from Ezekiel names Israel's wicked ways and corrupt doings. Those words are applied to this servant's conduct: he is corrupt, not a careful servant whose excuse makes him innocent. His knowledge of the lord's expectation exposes the contradiction in his defence.

“Wherefore then gavest not thou my money into the bank,” The bank is "this truth," the congregation, including the congregations in their different places. A servant can put his gift into the body's work instead of leaving it idle.

Romans explains that gifts differ and must be used according to the proportion of faith. Someone who can explain Deuteronomy 28 should do that rather than pretending to understand 2 Esdras 12. "But damn it, do something" is the practical point, not a demand to claim knowledge that has not been given.

Age and disability affect what work a person can do. The instruction expressly distinguishes elderly or disabled brothers from those refusing to use their abilities, and notes brothers in wheelchairs giving out flyers. The requirement is useful service with the capacity one actually has.

precepts.why:
“Now we beseech you, brethren, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, and by our gathering together unto him,” The subject is Christ's coming and our gathering to him, identified as the gathering of the twelve tribes. “That ye be not soon shaken in mind, or be troubled, neither by spirit, nor by word, nor by letter as from us, as that the day of Christ is at hand.” The believers must not be unsettled by a spirit, a word, or even a supposed letter from the apostles claiming that the day is already at hand.

“Let no man deceive you by any means: for that day shall not come, except there come a falling away first, and that man of sin be revealed, the son of perdition;” The falling away is explained as all twelve tribes falling into captivity. Judah, Benjamin, Levi, and remnants of the other tribes were still in the land, so that fall had not yet been completed. Christ's prediction of falling by the sword points to the Roman overthrow in AD 70.

The revealing of the man of sin is applied to the white ruling power being exposed as the devil in the teaching. These events had to precede the return. Paul therefore corrects the same impatience seen in Luke 19: the desired deliverance was not coming immediately, however unwelcome the news of intervening captivity might be.

“And when he had spoken these things, while they beheld, he was taken up; and a cloud received him out of their sight.” Christ is taken up while the disciples watch, and the cloud receives him out of their sight. This is the explanation of the nobleman going into a far country.

The destination is "the heavens to the true tabernacle," not a different province on earth. Read with the parable, the ascent supplies the departure before Christ receives the kingdom and returns. The servants are consequently given a charge to occupy during his absence. The promised return remains, but the parable includes this interval rather than the immediate appearance of the kingdom expected in verse 11.

“But thou, Israel, art my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen, the seed of Abraham my friend.” Israel is expressly named as the servant: Jacob whom God has chosen, the seed of Abraham his friend. The name answers who the servants in Luke's parable are.

The explanation rejects the assumption that the term automatically makes everyone on earth God's servant in the same sense. It is Israel who is being identified and entrusted with the work. The reading is followed by Leviticus naming the children of Israel brought out of Egypt, reinforcing the identification before the meaning of the ten pounds is explained. The charge to occupy belongs to that relationship and carries responsibility for using what the Lord gives.

“For unto me the children of Israel are servants; they are my servants whom I brought forth out of the land of Egypt: I am the Lord your God.” The children of Israel are God's servants, and the verse identifies them by the deliverance out of Egypt. That repeats and strengthens Isaiah's naming of Israel and Jacob as the servant.

The point is the identity of the ten servants in Luke 19. They are not left as an undefined group simply because the story is a parable. The Exodus and God's declaration "they are my servants" tie the charge to Israel. Once that identity is established, the reading returns to the pounds and the command to occupy: the people named as servants must put the entrusted understanding to work.

“Therefore I love thy commandments above gold; yea, above fine gold.” Pounds are money in the parable. This comparison with gold explains what that money represents: God's commandments, loved even above fine gold.

The entrusted pounds stand for something precious, the word of God and the understanding of his commandments. They are not merely cash placed with a servant for safekeeping. The return to Luke immediately continues with "Occupy till I come," so their value is connected to their use. When Christ later calls the servants to account, the question is what they have done with the understanding imparted to them.

“And he began to teach them, that the Son of man must suffer many things, and be rejected of the elders, and of the chief priests, and scribes,” The reading stops after naming those who reject Christ. The elders, chief priests, and scribes are the opponents used to explain the citizens who hate the nobleman.

The distinction is important: their rejection is not a statement that every Israelite rejected Christ. Using the language about his own not receiving him as an accusation against all Israel ignores the leaders specifically named here. Luke's citizens say they will not have this man reign over them; Mark clarifies the leadership expressing that refusal.

“For, behold, the Lord will come with fire, and with his chariots like a whirlwind, to render his anger with fury, and his rebuke with flames of fire.” “For by fire and by his sword will the Lord plead with all flesh: and the slain of the Lord shall be many.” The Lord's return brings fire, chariots, fury, and the sword; many are slain. These events explain what is compressed into the nobleman having received the kingdom. It is not simply a quiet arrival and an uncontested transfer of government.

“They that sanctify themselves, and purify themselves in the gardens behind one tree in the midst, eating swine’s flesh, and the abomination, and the mouse, shall be consumed together, saith the Lord.” The gardens are explained as religions and their churches. Swine's flesh means pork or hog; monkey hands, iguana, rat, rabbit stew, and possum stew are among the examples used in discussing the abomination and unclean food. The emphasis is that religious self-sanctification does not make those practices acceptable.

The return involves judgment before the kingdom is received. Revelation's account of war is read next to make that intervening conflict still more explicit.

“And there was war in heaven: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon; and the dragon fought and his angels,” Michael and his angels fight the dragon and his angels. Satan's opposing forces are applied to America, Europe, China, and Russia fighting against the Lord.

“And prevailed not; neither was their place found any more in heaven.” “And the great dragon was cast out, that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world: he was cast out into the earth, and his angels were cast out with him.” They do not prevail; the deceiver and his angels are cast down. The defeat is what makes the next declaration possible.

“And I heard a loud voice saying in heaven, Now is come salvation, and strength, and the kingdom of our God, and the power of his Christ: for the accuser of our brethren is cast down, which accused them before our God day and night.” Salvation, strength, the kingdom of God, and the power of Christ are announced after that conflict. That sequence explains Luke 19's short statement that the nobleman returned having received the kingdom. War and turmoil intervene before he calls his servants to account. The parable must be read with these prophecies rather than as though the current powers simply hand him their rule.

“Wherefore we labour, that, whether present or absent, we may be accepted of him.” The purpose of labour is to be accepted by Christ, present or absent. That is the work represented by the servants using the money entrusted to them while the nobleman is away.

“For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad.” Every man and every woman must appear before Christ's judgment seat. What each did in the body, good or bad, is answered for; the responsibility is not limited to the men explicitly depicted as servants in the story.

"What did you do with what I gave you?" is the question connecting the reading to Luke. Calling the servants to report their gain is the parable's account of that reckoning. Wanting acceptance must therefore be accompanied by actual labour, not merely possession of the gift.

“So then every one of us shall give account of himself to God.” The accounting is personal: every one of us answers to God. This follows the judgment-seat reading, which includes every man and woman and the things done in the body, whether good or bad.

In Luke, Christ calls the servants to learn how much each gained by trading. The money represents the understanding he imparted, so the reckoning concerns what each person did with that understanding. This verse reinforces that no one disappears inside the group at the time of judgment. The next reading about faithfulness in little then explains how that individual service bears on the greater responsibility represented by the cities.

“He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much.” Faithfulness in a small matter and faithfulness in a large one belong together; so do injustice in the least and injustice in much. The smallness of an entrusted responsibility does not make it insignificant.

Returning to the servant whose pound gained ten pounds, the lord calls him faithful in a very little and gives him authority over ten cities. His use of what he received is the evidence for that responsibility. The practical comparison with trying to put one's own household in order shows how much greater governing cities will be. Present service is the test, not something to postpone until larger authority arrives.

“And he that overcometh, and keepeth my works unto the end, to him will I give power over the nations:” Overcoming and keeping Christ's works to the end lead to power over the nations. That promise explains the authority over cities given to the faithful servant in Luke.

“And he shall rule them with a rod of iron; as the vessels of a potter shall they be broken to shivers:” The rod and the broken potter's vessels illustrate firm rule over resistance. Authority does not mean allowing people to continue refusing God's order.

The household example makes the scale concrete: if correcting an out-of-order family is difficult, organizing ten cities is much more demanding. They must learn dietary, moral, civil, and ceremonial law. People will resist, and their resistance must be brought under that rule. The reward is serious governing work, which is why the servant's faithfulness now matters.

“For whosoever hath, to him shall be given, and he shall have more abundance: but whosoever hath not, from him shall be taken away even that he hath.” The first half is attached to the second servant's gain of five pounds: the one who has receives more and has abundance. Productive use of what the lord gave is connected with increase.

Attention is then drawn to the second half, which will be developed in the next part of the parable. Even what a person has can be taken away. That prepares for the servant who leaves the pound in a napkin, makes excuses, and loses it. The contrast is not simply that one servant began richer than another; it is that the entrusted understanding was used or left idle.

“Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord;” The business is "God's business." Fervency in spirit and serving the Lord are contrasted with the servant's claim that he safely kept the pound laid up in a napkin.

Possessing the gift without using it is slothfulness, not faithful service. The reading is followed by the fruitless branch in John and the excuse-making sinner in Ecclesiasticus, keeping attention on the practical failure behind the napkin. The point is not to produce a clever explanation for inactivity but to do the work entrusted to us while Christ is away.

“Every branch in me that beareth not fruit he taketh away: and every branch that beareth fruit, he purgeth it, that it may bring forth more fruit.” The branch bearing no fruit is unproductive, and being taken away is explained bluntly: "He'll kill you." Hiding the pound is not a safe way to preserve a place while refusing useful work.

The productive branch is treated differently. Purging means trials, tribulations, and temptations, so that it may bring forth more fruit. Difficulty in the life of someone doing the work is therefore not the same as the removal of someone who bears nothing.

That distinction is brought back to the napkin in Luke 19. The servant should be using what was given and accepting the correction that makes it more fruitful, not defending an unused gift.

“A sinful man will not be reproved, but findeth an excuse according to his will.” "Them old excuse makers" is the description applied to the servant with the napkin. The sinner refuses reproof and finds a reason suited to his own will, rather than changing his conduct.

The return to Luke shows the excuse: he feared the lord because he was austere. The definition then makes that morally strict character plain. Knowing the lord's strictness is supposed to lead to service; the servant instead uses it to justify doing nothing. This is why his explanation is treated as resistance to correction, not a sound defence of faithfulness.

“And ye shall know that I am the Lord, when I have wrought with you for my name’s sake, not according to your wicked ways, nor according to your corrupt doings, O ye house of Israel, saith the Lord God.” The words singled out are Israel's "wicked ways" and "corrupt doings." They identify conduct that must be acknowledged as corrupt even when God deals with the house of Israel for his name's sake.

The immediate application is to the servant Christ calls wicked in Luke 19. He knew his lord was austere and still left the gift unused, then offered his own words as a defence. Being an Israelite does not make that behaviour righteous or remove the duty to work. The reading returns to the lord judging him from his own mouth and asking why the money was not placed in the bank.

“Having then gifts differing according to the grace that is given to us, whether prophecy, let us prophesy according to the proportion of faith;” Gifts differ according to grace, and prophecy must be exercised according to the proportion of faith. That explains how to place the pound in the bank, identified as the truth and the congregation: contribute the understanding and ability actually given.

If a brother can explain Deuteronomy 28, he should use that. He need not pretend to know 2 Esdras 12 or enter a passage he cannot explain. "But damn it, do something" is the instruction against sitting idle, not permission to teach beyond one's understanding.

Elderly brothers and those who are disabled or crippled are expressly distinguished from men making excuses. There may be other useful work suited to their capacity; brothers in wheelchairs giving out flyers are the example. Different gifts and limitations do not require identical tasks, but the congregation is where those real contributions can be put to use.

sense.text:
“But in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and of silver, but also of wood and of earth; and some to honour, and some to dishonour.” The great house is the twelve tribes of Israel, of which we are part. It contains vessels of gold and silver, but also wood and earth; some are to honour and others to dishonour.

The wood and earth are connected with the excuse-making servant who kept his gift in a napkin. His claim that he knew the lord was austere did not make him useful. Brothers and sisters can be in the truth yet bring dishonour through that spirit. Membership in the house does not remove the distinction between faithful service and excuses.

“If a man therefore purge himself from these, he shall be a vessel unto honour, sanctified, and meet for the master’s use,” Purging includes separating from dishonourable spirits. Examine the people in your circle: are they for your benefit or your detriment? Being fit for the Master's use requires more than remaining around people merely because they are called brothers or sisters.

The personal example is New York around 1990-1992: going down to 42nd Street and the clubs after class, jumping turnstiles, getting tickets, and repeatedly finding trouble. "I had to get the hell away from these dudes" is the conclusion about those companions. Choosing better company meant making an actual separation rather than expecting the same circle to produce a different result.

Women must make the same examination. A circle built on gossip, disrespect toward husbands, or neglect of children is harmful even when the person is a friend. The assumption that a decent sister will automatically change a rebellious one is answered by Proverbs: the wicked person's way can instead seduce her. Sanctified and "meet" means suitable or good for the Master's use; purging those influences helps make that possible.

precepts.why:
“The righteous is more excellent than his neighbour: but the way of the wicked seduceth them.” The first part names the righteous person's excellence, but the warning is in the second part: the wicked person's way seduces. Assuming that being righteous guarantees that your influence will win over every companion ignores that warning.

The example is a sister keeping close company with someone who gossips, disrespects her husband, or neglects her children. She thinks her scriptures will rub off on the hard-headed friend; instead, she begins carrying the same disrespect home. "It doesn't happen the other way" is the warning against confidently expecting that friendship to reform itself.

This explains purging oneself in 2 Timothy. Examine the circle for benefit or detriment and separate from the influence that keeps pulling you into wrong. The same lesson applies to the brothers repeatedly getting into trouble after class: a familiar companion is not necessarily good for the Master's work.

sense.text:
“Wherefore then gavest not thou my money into the bank, that at my coming I might have required mine own with usury?” Usury here means interest. Christ comes to collect what he entrusted and expects an increase: "what I gave you, you were supposed to multiply it."

The bank is the congregation and the work of the truth. Acts supplies an example involving literal money, unlike the understanding represented by the pound: people sold property, placed the proceeds with the apostles, and helped meet needs in the body. The explanation applies that support to people putting in work and to their families, not to the idle servant who leaves his gift wrapped up and demands help while contributing nothing.

“And he said unto them that stood by, Take from him the pound, and give it to him that hath ten pounds.” The pound is removed from the idle servant and given to the servant who already has ten. The objection is read too: “(And they said unto him, Lord, he hath ten pounds.)” Christ answers with the rule: “For I say unto you, That unto every one which hath shall be given; and from him that hath not, even that he hath shall be taken away from him.”

Matthew repeats the same principle. The explanation connects the pounds to the authority over cities: the servant with ten gained ten, the one with five gained five, and the unused pound is connected with the responsibility the idle servant should have received over one city. That responsibility is transferred to the one who proved productive.

The fact that the faithful servant already has much does not cancel the reward. What matters is the use made of the gift, not an equal reward for service and refusal to serve.

“But those mine enemies, which would not that I should reign over them, bring hither, and slay them before me.” The parable ends with judgment on enemies who refuse the nobleman's reign. It is the same morally strict lord described as austere, not a ruler who accepts permanent resistance to his authority.

The next question is who those enemies are among our people now. Romans 11 is opened to distinguish opposition concerning the gospel from the continuing possibility of repentance. Some who presently oppose the truth can still turn, as Paul did. That possibility must be understood without erasing the warning to those who persist in rejecting Christ's rule.

precepts.why:
“Neither was there any among them that lacked: for as many as were possessors of lands or houses sold them, and brought the prices of the things that were sold,” “And laid them down at the apostles’ feet: and distribution was made unto every man according as he had need.” Unlike the understanding represented by the pound in Luke, this example concerns literal lands, houses, and money. The proceeds are laid at the apostles' feet, then distributed where needs exist.

The explanation asks, "need for what?" and answers in terms of the work. Brothers putting in their bricks and doing the work, together with their families, need support. This is contrasted with someone arriving only to ask for money while doing nothing in the body.

That distinction ties the example back to the bank in the parable. Resources placed with the congregation can sustain useful work and help produce the increase Christ expects. It is not presented as approval of the napkin or a reward for an able servant who continually makes excuses.

“For whosoever hath, to him shall be given, and he shall have more abundance: but whosoever hath not, from him shall be taken away even that he hath.” This is read again when the pound is taken from the idle servant. The first reading anticipated the contrast; now Luke shows both parts in action, increase for the productive servant and loss for the one who did nothing.

The explanation relates the gain to cities. Ten pounds correspond to authority over ten cities, five to five, and the one unused pound to the responsibility the idle servant ought to have received. That responsibility is handed to the servant who already has ten.

The objection that he already possesses ten does not overturn the rule. Existing faithfulness is the reason he receives more, while keeping an unused gift does not secure it against removal.

sense.text:
“And so all Israel shall be saved: as it is written, There shall come out of Sion the Deliverer, and shall turn away ungodliness from Jacob:” The Deliverer coming out of Zion is Christ, and Jacob names the people whose ungodliness he removes. “For this is my covenant unto them, when I shall take away their sins.” The covenant concerns taking away their sins.

These words introduce the explanation of enemies within Israel after Luke's warning about refusing Christ's reign. Salvation is not permission for the people to remain ungodly. The following verses explain how people currently hostile to the gospel may still repent and receive what Christ has done for them.

“As concerning the gospel, they are enemies for your sakes: but as touching the election, they are beloved for the fathers’ sakes.” Enemies concerning the gospel are unbelievers among our own people. In Paul's time, the scribes, Pharisees, and Sadducees supplied the example; the application now is to brothers and sisters opposing the teaching while following Christianity, Islam, or other religions.

The answer that they are simply still Israelites is corrected as incomplete. The essential point is "they can still repent." Paul himself was an enemy of the gospel before the Lord allowed him to turn. Being beloved does not approve the hostility; it preserves the possibility that the hostile person can wake up and admit he has been wrong.

The prayer is that our brothers and sisters stop fighting, acknowledge the truth, and repent. The subsequent examples of faith leaders and urban apologists are offered as present opposition, including people described as having no congregations and seeking views and monetization. The same warning and opportunity apply: they are not to be followed in that opposition, but their repentance is still desired.

“For the gifts and calling of God are without repentance.” The explanation concerns the order of Christ's sacrifice and the people's repentance. Christ did not wait for them to repent first and then die on the cross. He died first; their opportunity to turn came afterward.

That is why current enemies can still be spoken of as beloved for the fathers' sakes. What Christ did already stands before their repentance, even for people who have not yet turned. It is not an argument that they never need to repent; it explains why the door remains open while the appeal is made to them.

“The wicked plotteth against the just, and gnasheth upon him with his teeth.” The just are our people. The wicked include the opposing nations and those among our own people who join them against the truth. Gnashing with the teeth is explained as evil speech: denying the Israelites' identity, insisting they are only Africans or Hamites, or changing the description of Christ from white to "Middle Eastern" or "an ethnic Jew" without explaining the terms.

The book Marks of a Lost Race is introduced as an example of alleged "crafty counsel." The objections are specific: the displayed name uses Bibbons rather than Bivens, the photograph is disputed, the editor is not recognized from the remembered school, and Change of Worlds is identified as the book known when the bishops entered. The claim that all nations could be saved is contrasted with the remembered teaching and audio of Abba Bivens.

The discussion also examines the claimed Northwestern library scan, the 1950 booklet, the 2023 independently published reprint, its extra pages, and who receives the proceeds from Amazon and Etsy. The suggested outside involvement is a suspicion, not something demonstrated by those publishing details. The point of the example is to challenge material used to undermine the teaching rather than accept its attributed authorship without examination.

“The Lord shall laugh at him: for he seeth that his day is coming.” The Lord laughs because he sees the day of judgment coming upon the wicked. Their plotting and apparent success do not put them beyond his view or make their counsel permanent.

Psalms 2 is later paired with this statement: rulers assemble against the Lord and his anointed, but the one in heaven laughs and then answers in wrath. The emphasis is the contrast between the confidence of those organizing opposition and the outcome already seen by God.

“The wicked have drawn out the sword, and have bent their bow, to cast down the poor and needy, and to slay such as be of upright conversation.” The drawn sword means war. The poor and needy are connected back to the afflicted people in Isaiah 61 and Luke 4:18, the people for whom the gospel announces release.

"Upright conversation" is applied to a way governed by the Bible: "Our conversation is in this book." The sword and bow are therefore presented as opposition not only to a people but to the righteous way they are learning. The following example of crafty counsel expands the discussion from open force to attempts to discredit that teaching.

precepts.why:
“Why do the heathen rage, and the people imagine a vain thing?” “The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the Lord, and against his anointed, saying,” The counsel against the Lord and his anointed is connected with opposition to Christ and the Israelites. It is read after the disputed book as the larger pattern into which such opposition is being placed.

“Let us break their bands asunder, and cast away their cords from us.” Breaking the bands is explained as breaking up the schools and tribes; casting away the cords is rejecting their teachings. The attack concerns the people being gathered and the instruction joining them together.

“He that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh: the Lord shall have them in derision.” “Then shall he speak unto them in his wrath, and vex them in his sore displeasure.” God laughs, holds the opponents in derision, and answers with wrath and displeasure. That is the same assurance as Psalms 37:13: he sees their day coming. The existence of organized counsel is not proof that it can prevail against him.

sense.text:
“As concerning the gospel, they are enemies for your sakes:” The return to this sentence develops the warning left after the earlier explanation. Gospel means good news; opposing that good news makes a person an enemy concerning it.

The possibility of repentance remains: these enemies are beloved in the sense that they can still turn. But what happens if they refuse?
