Proverbs answers that sinning against Christ wrongs one's own soul and hatred of him is love of death. Belonging to Israel cannot make continued hostility harmless or cancel that consequence.

precepts.why:
“But he that sinneth against me wrongeth his own soul: all they that hate me love death.” The words are applied to Christ: the person sinning against him harms his own soul, and those who hate him love death. "That's a cold deal right there" emphasizes the seriousness of the warning.

Romans has just explained that enemies concerning the gospel can still repent, as Paul did. That opportunity must not be confused with immunity if they refuse to turn. The reading answers precisely that question: what if they do not repent?

The next passage in Ezekiel makes the rebellion concrete through refusal of statutes and judgments and pollution of the Sabbath. Hostility is not merely a disagreement with another person; the warning concerns continued opposition to God's rule.

sense.text:
“Notwithstanding the children rebelled against me: they walked not in my statutes, neither kept my judgments to do them, which if a man do, he shall even live in them; they polluted my sabbaths: then I said, I would pour out my fury upon them, to accomplish my anger against them in the wilderness.” Israel's children rebel by not walking in the statutes, not keeping the judgments, and polluting the Sabbaths. "This is how you know you're an enemy of God" is the application to the opposition just described in Romans.

The fury is poured out in the wilderness. That setting matters when the reading moves to the future gathering: coming out among God's people does not remove the consequences of continuing in rebellion. The older wilderness history supplies the warning for the people who will be brought there again.

“As I live, saith the Lord God, surely with a mighty hand, and with a stretched out arm, and with fury poured out, will I rule over you:” The mighty hand, stretched-out arm, and fury describe rule that Israel cannot set aside. This is linked back to Luke 19 and its austere lord—morally strict, not a ruler who accepts a servant's excuse for refusing his commands.

The promise is not simply escape from another nation's authority so that each person can do as he pleases. The same Lord who gathers Israel declares that he will rule over them. Deliverance and submission to that government must be understood together.

“And I will bring you out from the people, and will gather you out of the countries wherein ye are scattered, with a mighty hand, and with a stretched out arm, and with fury poured out.” The people are gathered out of the countries where they are scattered. That identifies Israel as the subject, rather than treating all the nations from which they are brought as the same gathered people.

The repeated mighty hand, stretched-out arm, and fury connect this release with the authority of the preceding verse. The gathering is powerful, but it is not the end of the dealing with Israel. The following verses place the gathered people in the wilderness before their entry into the land.

“And I will bring you into the wilderness of the people, and there will I plead with you face to face.” “Like as I pleaded with your fathers in the wilderness of the land of Egypt, so will I plead with you, saith the Lord God.” The wilderness is identified as Egypt, the same place where the fathers were dealt with. The explanation is a return to that setting, not being taken directly into the land of Israel without further instruction and judgment.

The Lord pleading face to face is paired with Paul's contrast between seeing through a glass darkly and knowing face to face. The glass is the Bible; our present understanding is partial. Questions about what happens after the thousand-year reign or when the kingdom comes down must wait for answers not yet given, rather than be filled with guesses.

Paul's wilderness examples are then read at length. The old failures are an admonition for the generation upon whom the ends of the world come, because that generation will face this dealing again. The lesson is to learn now instead of repeating the rebellion when brought back to the wilderness.

“And I will cause you to pass under the rod, and I will bring you into the bond of the covenant:” Passing under the rod and coming into the bond of the covenant are explained as strict government. "Grace is over" describes the contrast with treating the present opportunity to repent as though another apology will always excuse repeated sin.

Adultery and theft supply the examples. The imagined response "My bad" does not set aside the future sentence; the adultery example is met with "Off with her head." The warning concerns the future wilderness judgment under Christ, not an instruction to listeners to administer punishment now. Learn from the fathers before that dealing comes, rather than assume deliverance cancels obedience.

“And I will purge out from among you the rebels, and them that transgress against me: I will bring them forth out of the country where they sojourn, and they shall not enter into the land of Israel: and ye shall know that I am the Lord.” Some rebels are brought out of the countries only to be purged in the wilderness and never enter Israel. Release from the country of captivity is therefore not proof that a person's journey is complete. Men, women, and children can all be among those resisting the order.

Luke's enemies who do not want Christ to reign are connected with this purging. The older examples are Moses and Aaron, then Joshua, and the seventy elders. The people wanted to hear God rather than Moses, then recoiled when faced with the thunder and the mountain. Rejecting appointed leaders while demanding to hear directly from God repeats that disorder.

The future illustration is Christ establishing the twelve and the 144 beneath them, teaching the order and leaving its administration with those appointed. A person who refuses that order cannot defend rebellion by insisting Christ must personally remain beside him all the time.

The wilderness comes before the land. God will make an example of rebels there, so the present instruction is to learn the lesson before being brought out. Isaiah's dryshod crossing and Zechariah's example of false prophecy develop the setting and the seriousness of that warning.

precepts.why:
“For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known.” The glass is explained as the Bible. We see through it darkly because we do not yet understand everything. The promised face-to-face understanding is connected with the Lord pleading with Israel face to face in Ezekiel's wilderness.

The examples of unanswered questions are what happens after the thousand-year reign and what happens when the kingdom comes down. Where the answer is not given, "We got to wait till the Lord come and ask him." He can explain what we now know only in part.

That is the purpose of this reading, not permission to invent details about the future. Ezekiel promises a time of direct dealing and instruction; Paul describes the difference between the present partial knowledge and that future understanding.

“Moreover, brethren, I would not that ye should be ignorant, how that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea;” “And were all baptized unto Moses in the cloud and in the sea;” Paul calls those under the cloud and through the sea "our fathers." This is used to identify the Corinthians being addressed as Israelites: their fathers are the people with Moses, not Greeks who were outside that Exodus.

“And did all eat the same spiritual meat;” “And did all drink the same spiritual drink: for they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ.” The spiritual food and drink culminate in the Rock identified as Christ. The Son, not merely the Father, was dealing with Israel as they came out of Egypt.

“But with many of them God was not well pleased: for they were overthrown in the wilderness.” “Now these things were our examples, to the intent we should not lust after evil things, as they also lusted.” Many were nevertheless overthrown. The warning is not to lust after evil as they did. “Neither be ye idolaters, as were some of them; as it is written, The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.” “Neither let us commit fornication, as some of them committed, and fell in one day three and twenty thousand.” Idolatry and fornication are specified, including the twenty-three thousand who fell in one day.

“Neither let us tempt Christ, as some of them also tempted, and were destroyed of serpents.” “Neither murmur ye, as some of them also murmured, and were destroyed of the destroyer.” The serpents and the destroyer answer tempting Christ and murmuring. The naming of Christ is emphasized again against the assumption that the Son was absent from those events.

“Now all these things happened unto them for ensamples: and they are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come.” Ensamples means examples. The repeated warning concerns the generation upon whom the ends of the world have come, not only people in Paul's immediate time. The application is that we return to the wilderness described in Ezekiel and must learn from the fathers now. National deliverance does not make the same old rebellion safe.

“And the Lord shall utterly destroy the tongue of the Egyptian sea; and with his mighty wind shall he shake his hand over the river, and shall smite it in the seven streams, and make men go over dryshod.” Dryshod means on dry land. The tongue of the Egyptian sea, the mighty wind, and the river smitten into seven streams describe God making a way for the people to cross.

The comparison is with the earlier Exodus: the Red Sea parted and Israel crossed on dry ground. The same kind of event is expected again, so this reading supports the return to the wilderness of Egypt described in Ezekiel.

The point is a real stage in the return, not only a metaphor about personal feelings. Israel is brought to the wilderness, dealt with there, and then goes into the land. The miraculous crossing shows God's power making that journey possible while the preceding warning still distinguishes those allowed to enter from the rebels purged out.

“In that day there shall be a fountain opened to the house of David and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem for sin and for uncleanness.” The fountain is Christ, opened to the house of David and Jerusalem for sin and uncleanness. Cleansing and forgiveness are the opening promise.

“And it shall come to pass in that day, saith the Lord of hosts, that I will cut off the names of the idols out of the land, and they shall no more be remembered: and also I will cause the prophets and the unclean spirit to pass out of the land.” Idols, the prophets associated with falsehood, and the unclean spirit are removed. Restoration is not permission to preserve the old idolatry under a new government.

“And it shall come to pass, that when any shall yet prophesy, then his father and his mother that begat him shall say unto him, Thou shalt not live; for thou speakest lies in the name of the Lord: and his father and his mother that begat him shall thrust him through when he prophesieth.” The example is interpreted as a rebellious child continuing to prophesy lies, illustrated by persisting in claims about Santa Claus and a white Jesus. The parents' severe judgment is connected with the rebels in Ezekiel 20, including children as well as adults.

This is presented as the future purging, not an instruction to listeners to punish children now. It explains why the warnings in 1 Corinthians 10 matter for those who will return to that setting. Deliverance and cleansing do not protect continuing rebellion from the Lord's judgment.

sense.text:
“I am the God of thy fathers, the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are the fathers named in the biblical account. The reading starts here deliberately before moving to the church in the wilderness.

The discussion of "church fathers" is redirected from later religious authorities to these named patriarchs. The immediate setting is the response to a video criticizing Black church identity. Instead of accepting an undefined claim about who the people of God are, the answer begins with the fathers actually named in scripture.

“This is that Moses, which said unto the children of Israel, A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you of your brethren, like unto me; him shall ye hear.” Moses addresses the children of Israel, and the promised prophet comes from their brethren. Christ is the prophet they must hear.

The reading joins the fathers named above to the people in the wilderness below. Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the children of Israel, Moses, and the promised prophet form the sequence being used to establish the identity of the church. The argument does not begin with the names of later denominations.

“This is he, that was in the church in the wilderness with the angel” The church in the wilderness is the twelve tribes of Israel with Moses. That is the assembly being identified, following the naming of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and the prophet raised up from Israel's brethren.

Baptist, Pentecostal, and Catholic institutions are rejected as replacements for that biblical identity. The response to the claim that other nations were present is that those others were Israel's slaves, not a reason to change the identity of the church itself.

The preceding video objected to speaking of Black churches and described racial loyalty as "ethnic idolatry." The response points to the exclusion of Black people by white churches and to white images behind the critics. Acts supplies the scriptural answer to the identity question instead of accepting those criticisms as its starting point.

“And Jesus answered and said unto them, Take heed that no man deceive you.” “For many shall come in my name, saying, I am Christ; and shall deceive many.” Coming in Christ's name can be the vehicle for deception, so a claim to represent him is not enough to establish truth.

The application is to Europeans painting over Black images and presenting themselves in the image of Christ. "I am Christ" is connected with that substitution. The warning then leads directly into Revelation 13: conquest of the saints and worldwide worship are read together to explain how the conquering power's image became religious authority. The point is to recognize the deception instead of treating the familiar image as proof.

“And it was given unto him to make war with the saints, and to overcome them: and power was given him over all kindreds, and tongues, and nations.” The power making war and overcoming the saints is identified with the white conquering power. The saints are not left undefined: Psalms is opened to identify them as the children of Israel.

The conquest extends into power over kindreds, tongues, and nations. Read after Matthew's warning about deception in Christ's name, it explains why the religious image cannot be separated from the rule of the power spreading it. The following verse is applied to the same man being worshipped after overcoming our people.

“And all that dwell upon the earth shall worship him, whose names are not written in the book of life of the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world.” The worldwide worship is connected to the conquering power just described, while those written in the Lamb's book of life are distinguished from it.

The displayed book is The Pillory: The Tale of the Borgia Pope in Nine Crowded Chapters, attributed to John Bond and dated 1920 in the discussion. Its text and the bust shown are used to argue that Cesare Borgia, son of Pope Alexander, posed for the European image presented as the Saviour. The image's "Salvator" wording is explained as saviour, and the same argument is applied to a white Jesus pendant.

The example illustrates the claim that the conqueror's image has been received as Christ. It does not close the possibility of repentance: our people worshipping that image can still wake up out of the deception. That opportunity is stated before the reading moves to the clip about responsibility for slavery.

precepts.why:
“He also exalteth the horn of his people, the praise of all his saints; even of the children of Israel,” The reading stops after the identification of the saints with the children of Israel. That is the name needed to understand the people against whom war is made in Revelation 13.

The explanation explicitly excludes Edomite, Philistine, and Moabite saints in this interpretation. The word is not being used for everyone claiming a religious title. It concerns Israel, the people overcome by the conquering power.

Returning to Revelation, the same power that makes war on those saints receives authority over kindreds, tongues, and nations and becomes the object of worldwide worship. Keeping the identity from Psalms makes the conquest and the subsequent image discussion part of one argument.

sense.text:
“The inheritance of sinners’ children shall perish, and their posterity shall have a perpetual reproach.” “The children will complain of an ungodly father, because they shall be reproached for his sake.” The children inherit reproach connected with their ungodly father. This is read in answer to a video in which a Christian theologian refuses guilt for the transatlantic slave trade because he did not personally commit it.

The interviewer contrasts that refusal with taking pride in Britain's defeat of the Nazis, another event the individual did not personally accomplish. The exchange over pride, admiration, and guilt is used to expose the inconsistency being challenged.

The added point is that descendants remain direct beneficiaries of their forefathers' wrongdoing, described in the discussion as the benefits of four hundred years of free slave labour. Belonging to a later generation does not erase the inherited advantage or the reproach attached to it. Isaiah is then read as the paired example of consequences reaching the children.

precepts.why:
“Prepare slaughter for his children for the iniquity of their fathers; that they do not rise, nor possess the land, nor fill the face of the world with cities.” The consequences for the children are expressly connected with the iniquity of their fathers. Their rising, possessing the land, and filling the world with cities are the outcomes the verse says are prevented.

Read with Ecclesiasticus, it answers the claim that a descendant has no connection at all with the oppression of an earlier generation. The discussion emphasizes inherited benefit: the descendants still profit from the wealth and position produced by that wrongdoing, while rejecting any reproach for it.

The severity is attributed to the judgment stated in scripture—"That's what God said"—rather than presented as a personal instruction to listeners. The pair of readings is used to join inherited advantage with the biblical language of inherited consequence.

sense.text:
“And in those times there shall many stand up against the king of the south: also the robbers of thy people shall exalt themselves to establish the vision; but they shall fall.” The king of the south is identified as Egypt. The robbers are identified in this interpretation as Amalek in the land of Israel, exalting themselves as the Jews and seeking to establish the claim that they are God's people and that the land is theirs.

The immediate context is the Christian Zionist pastors' visit to Israel: an eight-day programme, meetings with officials and military leaders, advocacy training, and commissioning as Friends of Zion ambassadors. The discussion argues that funding and political instruction compromise those pastors and prepare them to oppose Israelite teaching. The reported plan to reach a million pastors and a claimed enlarged 2026 publicity budget are examples of the scale being criticized, not separate biblical identifications.

The conclusion rests on "but they shall fall." The stated reason not to be consumed with worry over those campaigns is the expected outcome of the prophecy. The following examples, including the comparison of "Jewish derangement syndrome" with the slavery-era invention of drapetomania, continue the argument about labelling opposition instead of answering it.

“Associate yourselves, O ye people, and ye shall be broken in pieces; and give ear, all ye of far countries: gird yourselves, and ye shall be broken in pieces; gird yourselves, and ye shall be broken in pieces.” Association with powerful allies does not make an opposing plan secure. The repeated warning that they will be broken in pieces answers the confidence placed in such an alliance.

The application is specifically to Black and Latino pastors joining other powers against the Israelite teaching. The preceding chapter is read to establish the comparison: Ephraim joined Syria against its own brothers in Judah. Shared ancestry does not mean every alliance our people enter serves their brothers or the truth.

“Take counsel together, and it shall come to nought; speak the word, and it shall not stand: for God is with us.” Taking counsel and speaking a word against God's people do not guarantee that either will stand. The reason given is that God is with us, identified here as the Israelites.

The pastors' journey to Israel is applied as a present example of taking counsel together. Their numbers, access, and official backing cannot overturn God's declaration. Isaiah 7's rejected plan against Judah supplies the historical comparison for this confidence, rather than the claim that alliances are powerful enough to decide the outcome by themselves.

“For the Lord spake thus to me with a strong hand, and instructed me that I should not walk in the way of this people,” The instruction is not to follow the way of our wicked people merely because they are our people.

In the preceding comparison, the northern kingdom's shared ancestry with Judah did not make its alliance with Syria righteous. The present application is the same: do not follow leaders joining outside powers against the truth. God's instruction, not the association or the prestige of those taking counsel, determines where to walk.

precepts.why:
“Because Syria, Ephraim, and the son of Remaliah, have taken evil counsel against thee, saying,” “Let us go up against Judah, and vex it, and let us make a breach therein for us, and set a king in the midst of it, even the son of Tabeal:” Syria, Ephraim, and the son of Remaliah plan to attack Judah, breach it, and install the son of Tabeal as king. The northern kingdom joins an outside power against its own brothers.

“Thus saith the Lord God, It shall not stand, neither shall it come to pass.” God's answer is that the plan will not stand or come to pass. That is the background used to explain the associations and counsel in Isaiah 8, rather than reading those verses without their preceding conflict.

The application is to our people joining other nations against the truth today, particularly the pastors whose visit and advocacy have just been discussed. An alliance does not become righteous through shared ancestry, and its strength does not overturn God's declared outcome. This is also why the instruction is not to walk in that people's way.

sense.text:
“Wherefore hear the word of the Lord, ye scornful men, that rule this people which is in Jerusalem.” The scornful rulers are applied to pastors who have the ear of Black and brown communities. Not every person listens to them, but their influence helps explain why outside powers seek their support.

That setting leads into the covenant of verse 15. Leaders with an audience can bring an agreement and its message back to the people, so the warning begins with those ruling and speaking to Jerusalem rather than treating their influence as morally neutral.

“Because ye have said, We have made a covenant with death, and with hell are we at agreement; when the overflowing scourge shall pass through, it shall not come unto us: for we have made lies our refuge, and under falsehood have we hid ourselves:” The covenant with death is applied to the pastors' agreement with the white ruling power through their visit to Israel. The agreement with hell is connected to the hellish condition of our own people and, in the immediate illustration, to supporting a government accused in the discussion of mass killing in Gaza.

The belief that the overflowing scourge will not reach them is confidence that the alliance will spare them when judgment comes. Lies as a refuge and falsehood as a hiding place are applied to Christian Zionism and the claims used to defend that agreement.

The distinction is between a refuge that appears politically useful and the foundation God actually provides in the next verse. The agreement does not remove the condition of our people or secure exemption from judgment.

“Therefore thus saith the Lord God, Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation: he that believeth shall not make haste.” The tried stone, precious corner stone, and sure foundation are Christ. He is the leader and the foundation on which belief must rest, rather than the covenant with death described above.

The person who believes does not make haste to leave the truth. A quick departure is taken as evidence that the person never had that settled belief. The point is steadfast trust in Christ instead of seeking security in the alliance and falsehood exposed in the preceding verse.

“Judgment also will I lay to the line, and righteousness to the plummet: and the hail shall sweep away the refuge of lies, and the waters shall overflow the hiding place.” Judgment and righteousness replace the supposed security of lies. The hail is destruction sweeping away the refuge, and the waters are destruction overflowing the hiding place.

The application includes the religious falsehood just described and the physical bunkers in which people may expect safety. Neither can keep God's judgment outside. This is the answer to the confidence of verse 15 that the overflowing scourge will not reach those sheltered by the agreement.

“And your covenant with death shall be disannulled, and your agreement with hell shall not stand; when the overflowing scourge shall pass through, then ye shall be trodden down by it.” The covenant is disannulled and the agreement does not stand. Applied to Black and Latino people joining the white ruling power, the warning is that the association cannot preserve them when the scourge arrives.

The "hell" is again connected with our hellish condition. Joining an agreement within that condition does not bring the promised liberation or shield the participants from judgment. Proverbs reinforces this with the warning that joining hand in hand does not prevent the wicked from being punished.

“From the time that it goeth forth it shall take you: for morning by morning shall it pass over, by day and by night: and it shall be a vexation only to understand the report.” The morning-by-morning, day-and-night report is applied to teaching seven days a week. People opposing it are vexed even by understanding what the Bible is actually saying, because it exposes the falsehood in what they have followed.

The practical instruction is to "teach right and keep it moving." State what the Bible says and what it means; do not remain trapped in endless debates with those refusing the report. The repeated teaching itself carries the warning, even when hearing and understanding it makes the opponents angry.

“For the bed is shorter than that a man can stretch himself on it: and the covering narrower than that he can wrap himself in it.” The short bed is Christianity in this application. A man cannot stretch out and be comfortable on a bed too short for him. The narrow covering represents the same religion: it cannot wrap him adequately or give the comfort he expects.

The two images explain the failure of the refuge sought in the preceding verses. The problem is not solved by trying harder to make the inadequate bed or covering fit. The promised comfort of the gospel cannot be supplied by the religious shelter being criticized.

“For the Lord shall rise up as in mount Perazim, he shall be wroth as in the valley of Gibeon, that he may do his work, his strange work; and bring to pass his act, his strange act.” Mount Perazim and the valley of Gibeon introduce the Lord rising in wrath. His return is described with anger, fury, and flames of fire.

The "strange work" and "strange act" are explained as the destruction of the opposing nations and the deliverance of the twelve tribes who believe on him. People who expected something very different will be shocked. This connects the passage back to the theme of liberation through judgment rather than the belief that the present alliances will secure peace and exemption.

“Now therefore be ye not mockers, lest your bands be made strong: for I have heard from the Lord God of hosts a consumption, even determined upon the whole earth.” Consumption is explained as destruction, determined upon the whole earth. The warning not to be mockers is addressed to the brothers and sisters hearing it as well as to the people being criticized.

Mocking does not weaken what God has determined; it makes the bands strong. The conclusion is therefore to take the warning seriously, rather than imagine that laughter, argument, or a powerful agreement can remove the coming judgment.

precepts.why:
“Though hand join in hand, the wicked shall not be unpunished: but the seed of the righteous shall be delivered.” Joining hand in hand does not spare the wicked from punishment. The Lord's judgment is not cancelled by the identity or power of an ally.

That is the direct answer to Isaiah's covenant with death. The pastors' alliance and its promises of protection are treated as misplaced confidence, not a way of securing the people against the overflowing scourge. Joining another wicked party cannot make one's own conduct safe.

The other side of the verse is also read: the seed of the righteous is delivered. The distinction is righteousness and wickedness, not being able to find the strongest political or religious partner. The closing reading in Jeremiah extends that accountability across the nations.

sense.text:
“For thus saith the Lord God of Israel unto me; Take the wine cup of this fury at my hand, and cause all the nations, to whom I send thee, to drink it.” The wine cup is a metaphor for the prophecy Jeremiah must carry. Taking it from the Lord and causing the nations to drink means going to them and declaring the judgment.

Their willingness to receive the message does not determine whether he must speak. "Whether they accept it or not. Prophesy" is the instruction drawn from the image. The later warning that they will certainly drink returns to this same distinction between hearing a prophecy and being able to cancel its fulfilment.

“And they shall drink, and be moved, and be mad, because of the sword that I will send among them.” The nations hear the proclamation, are moved, and become angry. The sword is explained as war, the judgment announced against them.

“Then took I the cup at the Lord’s hand, and made all the nations to drink, unto whom the Lord had sent me:” Jeremiah taking the cup and giving it to the nations means he prophesied as commanded. The image describes the delivery of God's word, not Jeremiah literally carrying wine between countries. The following list identifies where the proclamation is directed.

“To wit, Jerusalem, and the cities of Judah, and the kings thereof, and the princes thereof, to make them a desolation, an astonishment, an hissing, and a curse; as it is this day;” Jerusalem is the first destination, together with Judah's cities, kings, and princes. Desolation, astonishment, hissing, and a curse describe the judgment announced there.

“Pharaoh king of Egypt, and his servants, and his princes, and all his people;” Pharaoh and Egypt follow, including servants, princes, and people. The sequence matters at the later question in verse 29: if God begins by punishing the city called by his name, the other nations cannot assume that they alone will remain unpunished.

“And all the mingled people, and all the kings of the land of Uz, and all the kings of the land of the Philistines, and Ashkelon, and Azzah, and Ekron, and the remnant of Ashdod,” The mingled people are identified as Keturah's children in the Middle East. Uz is identified with modern Jordan, and the land of the Philistines with Palestine.

A modern map is requested to answer the objection that these are merely obsolete names. Ashkelon is pointed out as Ashqelon above Gaza; Azzah is identified as Gaza, with attention to the name's spelling; Ekron is pointed out near Jerusalem and Ashdod beside it on the displayed map.

The purpose is to connect the names in the prophecy with places recognizable on a contemporary map. The list is not passed over as irrelevant simply because some spellings or modern labels differ.

“Edom, and Moab, and the children of Ammon,” Edom is identified with Jordan, Moab with China, and the children of Ammon with the Japanese. These are the identifications supplied while applying the list to the present nations.

“And all the kings of Tyrus, and all the kings of Zidon, and the kings of the isles which are beyond the sea,” Tyrus and Zidon are identified as modern Lebanon, followed by the kings of the isles beyond the sea. These places and peoples remain part of the wider point: the cup is directed beyond Judah to the surrounding nations and then across the earth, not only to Israel.

“Dedan, and Tema, and Buz, and all that are in the utmost corners,” “And all the kings of Arabia, and all the kings of the mingled people that dwell in the desert,” Dedan, Tema, Buz, and the utmost corners are connected with the Arabs, with the next verse explicitly naming Arabia. The mingled people dwelling in the desert are identified as Keturah's children.

“And all the kings of Zimri, and all the kings of Elam, and all the kings of the Medes,” Zimri is also assigned to Keturah's children; Elam is identified with Pakistan and India, and the Medes with Iran. Genesis 25 is mentioned while making those identifications, but the reading remains in Jeremiah's list.

The application continues the roll call of peoples receiving the cup. No one is removed from that judgment merely because the ancient name first needs explaining.

“And all the kings of the north, far and near, one with another, and all the kingdoms of the world, which are upon the face of the earth: and the king of Sheshach shall drink after them.” The kings of the north are applied to NATO, with France and Germany named as examples; Russia is then expressly added because it is northward. The wider phrase about all kingdoms covers those not individually named in the list.

Sheshach is identified as the United States of America, drinking after the other kingdoms. Jeremiah 51 is read to show Sheshach and Babylon named together. With Babylon applied to America, the parallel supplies the identification used here.

The point is that the reach of the cup is worldwide. The final kingdom's position in the sequence is not an exemption from having to drink.

“Therefore thou shalt say unto them, Thus saith the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel; Drink ye, and be drunken, and spue, and fall, and rise no more, because of the sword which I will send among you.” The command to drink, fall, and rise no more is tied to the sword that God sends among the nations. The sword has already been explained as war.

“And it shall be, if they refuse to take the cup at thine hand to drink, then shalt thou say unto them, Thus saith the Lord of hosts; Ye shall certainly drink.” Refusing to take the cup is applied to refusing to hear Jeremiah's prophecy. That refusal cannot cancel it. "Ye shall certainly drink" means the announced judgment still comes whether the hearers accept the words or reject them. Their anger at the messenger does not give them authority over the outcome.

“For, lo, I begin to bring evil on the city which is called by my name, and should ye be utterly unpunished? Ye shall not be unpunished: for I will call for a sword upon all the inhabitants of the earth, saith the Lord of hosts.” The city called by God's name is Jerusalem. The force of the question is: if he punished his own people, why should the other nations imagine that they will be utterly unpunished?

The answer is emphatic that they will not escape. The sword is called upon all the inhabitants of the earth, connecting this verse to the full list just read. The verse is singled out as useful in street teaching because it answers the assumption that Israel's punishment leaves the nations beyond God's judgment.

“Therefore prophesy thou against them all these words, and say unto them, The Lord shall roar from on high, and utter his voice from his holy habitation; he shall mightily roar upon his habitation; he shall give a shout, as they that tread the grapes, against all the inhabitants of the earth.” Jeremiah must prophesy these words against the nations and countries just named. The Lord's roar from his holy habitation and the shout associated with treading grapes announce the judgment reaching all the earth's inhabitants.

“A noise shall come even to the ends of the earth; for the Lord hath a controversy with the nations, he will plead with all flesh; he will give them that are wicked to the sword, saith the Lord.” The controversy is with the nations, and the wicked are given to the sword. The application includes those among our own people who join the opposition, not only outsiders.

This brings the conclusion back to the title's understanding of the gospel: liberation, glad tidings, and good news for Black people. Ending oppression includes an accounting for the powers that maintained it, which is why the proclamation of judgment is joined to the hope of deliverance.

“Thus saith the Lord of hosts, Behold, evil shall go forth from nation to nation, and a great whirlwind shall be raised up from the coasts of the earth.” The evil going from nation to nation and the great whirlwind are explained as destruction with the chariots. The scale is worldwide, matching the countries and peoples named throughout the passage.

“And the slain of the Lord shall be at that day from one end of the earth even unto the other end of the earth: they shall not be lamented, neither gathered, nor buried; they shall be dung upon the ground.” The slain stretch from one end of the earth to the other. The details are emphasized separately: not lamented, not gathered, not buried, but left as dung on the ground.

The closing declaration returns to the twelve tribes and to the gospel as Black liberation. The conclusion is the expected end of the powers oppressing them, the deliverance connected throughout the reading to God's appointed judgment. As with the earlier mourning passage, that expectation concerns the Lord's intervention, not a command for listeners to initiate violence.

Its description as the praise of the whole earth, now taken and an astonishment among the nations, supplies the link between those names.

With Babylon identified as the United States of America in the application, Sheshach is likewise identified as America in Jeremiah 25. That is why this verse is read immediately after the statement that Sheshach drinks after the other kingdoms.

The return to Jeremiah 25 adds Russia to the northern countries already associated with NATO and then continues to the command to drink. The list embraces the whole earth, and its final position does not exempt Sheshach from the judgment announced to the others.
